title: You Did Not Learn That With AI
author: The Slow AI
summary: The author reports on a summer 2026 study from Sungkyunkwan University finding that students who leaned hardest on AI during problem-solving reported the highest perceived learning and satisfaction while scoring lowest on an objective test measuring what they'd actually learned. The piece argues that reaching for 'Dunning-Kruger' to explain this gets it only half right, since the classic effect describes miscalibrated confidence in the unskilled, whereas this new finding shows the false confidence is manufactured by the tool itself, not the learner's pre-existing skill level. It explains that the 'click' of a good AI explanation feels like understanding because it is fluent and well-pitched, but that fluency substitutes for the effortful retrieval and struggle that actually build competence. The piece previews a four-move protocol (reserved for paid subscribers) and cites a separate four-university, 1,176-student trial showing that a single change to task ordering protected students' independent ability once the AI tool was removed.
points: A 2026 study found students who relied most heavily on AI during problem-solving scored lowest on objective tests despite reporting the highest perceived learning and satisfaction.
This is not simply the classic Dunning-Kruger effect: the false confidence here is manufactured by the AI tool's fluency, not by the learner's pre-existing lack of skill.

A good AI explanation produces the 'click' of understanding because it is optimized to be coherent and well-pitched — but that click is not the same as the effortful retrieval that builds real competence.
A student can do all the assigned reading, feel the 'click' with AI, and still walk out with less durable learning than a peer who struggled without it.
A separate trial across four universities and 1,176 students found that changing the order of a task alone protected students' capability once the AI tool was taken away.
quotes: That feeling has stopped being evidence that you have learnt anything of value.
Students who used AI during problem solving scored higher on the later test than students who used it only for concept understanding.
the students who leaned on the tool hardest scored lower on the objective test while reporting higher perceived learning and higher satisfaction.
Generative AI is a powerful tool that increases learning efficiency, but relying on it uncritically can lead to the paradoxical result of lowering objective academic achievement.
You get the sensation of learning without the process that causes it.
A student can use AI exactly as permitted, do all the reading, feel the click, and walk out with less than the student who struggled.
